binders: For every natural number m ≥ 0, let V = {v : Fin m → R}, identified with R^m.
For every function q : R → R → V, with q(x,t) denoting its value at spatial coordinate x and time coordinate t.
For every function flux : V → V.
For every function fluxDerivative : V → L_R(V,V), where L_R(V,V) consists of continuous real-linear endomorphisms of V.
For every x,t ∈ R and every supplied vector qx ∈ V.
On the left of the equivalence, there exist qt ∈ V and then fluxx ∈ V, with the latter witness in the scope of qt.

On the right of the equivalence, there exist qt ∈ V and then v ∈ V, where v renames the locally bound qx to distinguish it from the supplied outer qx. Witnesses on the two sides are independently quantified and may depend on the fixed outer data.
hypotheses: The function ξ ↦ q(ξ,t) has derivative qx at x.
The function flux has Fréchet derivative fluxDerivative(q(x,t)) at the state q(x,t).
conclusions: The following assertions are equivalent: (A) there exist qt, fluxx ∈ V such that τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative qt at t, ξ ↦ flux(q(ξ,t)) has derivative fluxx at x, and qt + fluxx = 0; (B) there exist qt, v ∈ V such that τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative qt at t, ξ ↦ q(ξ,t) has derivative v at x, and qt + fluxDerivative(q(x,t))(v) = 0.
The equation in (A) means qt(i) + fluxx(i) = 0 for every i ∈ Fin m. The equation in (B) means qt(i) + [fluxDerivative(q(x,t))(v)](i) = 0 for every i ∈ Fin m.
mathematical_definitions: V has pointwise real vector operations and the product topology, which is the usual finite-dimensional topology on R^m.
For a curve f : R → V, having derivative w at a means f(a+h) = f(a) + h w + o(|h|) as h → 0.

For flux : V → V, having Fréchet derivative A at u means flux(u+h) = flux(u) + A(h) + o(‖h‖) as h → 0, with A continuous and real-linear. Any norm inducing the finite-dimensional topology gives the same derivative notion.
LocalDef001 is the existence-based assertion that the time derivative of q and the spatial derivative of the composed flux exist at the fixed point and sum to zero.

LocalDef002 is the existence-based assertion that the time and spatial derivatives of q exist at the fixed point and that the time derivative plus the supplied state-dependent linear map applied to the spatial derivative is zero.
Under the hypotheses, the composed-flux spatial derivative is fluxDerivative(q(x,t))(qx), and any spatial derivative witness v in (B) equals the outer qx by uniqueness of derivatives.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every nonnegative finite dimension m, every real vector-valued function q of two real variables, every flux function on R^m, every assignment fluxDerivative of continuous real-linear endomorphisms to states, every point (x,t), and every vector qx, assume that q has spatial derivative qx at (x,t) and that flux is Fréchet differentiable at q(x,t) with derivative fluxDerivative(q(x,t)). Then existence of a time derivative of q and a spatial derivative of flux composed with q whose sum is zero at (x,t) is equivalent to existence of time and spatial derivatives of q at (x,t) for which the time derivative plus fluxDerivative(q(x,t)) applied to the spatial derivative is zero. Both assertions include existence of the time derivative; neither is asserted to hold unconditionally.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The dimension is finite, but it need not be positive. When m = 0, V contains only the empty vector; the derivatives and zero-vector equations are trivial, and both sides hold.
The independent variables range over all real numbers. There is no restriction to positive time, a spatial interval, a boundary, or a specified subset.
All derivative assertions concern full neighborhoods of the specified point. No within-domain, one-sided, weak, or distributional derivative is encoded.

The assumptions are local: spatial differentiability of q is required only at x with t fixed, and differentiability of flux only at q(x,t). Joint differentiability of q, continuity of its derivatives, and differentiability on an entire region are not required.

The type of fluxDerivative requires each value to be a continuous linear map, but does not require continuity of the assignment of maps to states or identify it with the derivative of flux away from q(x,t).
Time differentiability is not an outer hypothesis or an unconditional conclusion. If the time derivative fails to exist at the point, both predicates are false and their equivalence still holds.
If either outer derivative hypothesis fails, the conditional theorem imposes no equivalence for those data.

The theorem does not assert existence of a solution q, satisfaction of either equation at every point, initial or boundary conditions, an integral conservation law, or any spectral or hyperbolicity property of the linear map.

The existential spatial derivative on the right is not syntactically identified with the outer qx, although the derivative hypotheses force equality. The conclusion supplies no globally chosen derivative fields.
